results.why: It names sync-payments overwriting paid_at as an edge case and proposes a handling for it, so the second writer is covered. The migration has a down step and an up/down/up test. It flags the cleanup conflict with AC4 but recommends the fix and lists it as plan step 5, so it chose rather than leaving the decision open. Tests are grouped into one section instead of coming first in each task, and each task does not have its own failing test. No invented requirements.

It handles syncPayments re-settlement and orders the archive job after syncPayments. The migration has a down step, and the plan tests up/down on an in-memory DB or checks it by hand. It recommends a fix for the cleanup conflict instead of leaving the choice to the user. Tests are not written first per task. No invented requirements.

It raises re-settlement by syncPayments as an open question. It flags the cleanup conflict and says plainly 'I haven't picked one'. The migration down is only weakly tested: an optional real-DB test plus a manual check. Tests are not written first per task. Its claim that void rows always have a NULL paid_at is not supported: the schema allows paid_at on any row, and no file shows that void rows lack it.

This is a full test-first plan: every task names its files and starts with a failing test and the command that shows it failing. The migration down is tested properly with node:sqlite, and the attempt confirmed node:sqlite is available by running a command. It includes a test for an archived invoice re-settled by syncPayments. It flags the cleanup conflict as needing a decision, but Task 4 already builds the guard, so it effectively chose.

It wrote no plan file and stopped to ask questions. It lays out cleanup options but recommends option 1. It never treats sync-payments as a second writer. It mentions a down step but no test for it, and gives no per-task test-first steps. The questions it asks are reasonable, but it did not do the task it was given.

Each task lists its files and starts with a failing test, with a run step that expects FAIL. The sync-payments rewrite of paid_at on archived rows is named in Review Focus, and the plan says archived_at must stay untouched. The migration has a down step, but no task tests it. The cleanup conflict is not left open: Task 3 builds the archived_at guard unconditionally, and the user is only asked afterwards whether that is intended. The scheduler and DB-version questions are extra; both are supported by the files the attempt read.

Step 4 deals with sync-payments directly: it rewrites paid_at, the re-settled-archived case is called out, and the plan recommends leaving archived_at alone. The down migration is planned with an up/down/up test where a real driver exists. The cleanup step is held until the user decides and an alternative is offered, but the plan still proposes a specific fix. Tests are bunched into step 6 at the end, not written failing first for each task.

It identifies sync-payments rewriting paid_at, rules that it must not clear archived_at, and orders the job after syncPayments. The down step is checked with an up/down/up round trip on a scratch DB. The steps are labelled test-first, but no task gives a concrete failing test with a run that is expected to fail. On cleanup, step 4 builds the guard and the open question only asks for the user's OK, so the plan has effectively already chosen.

Re-payment through markPaid and syncPayments is raised as an open issue with a proposed handling. The cleanup fix is held until the user signs off and retiring the job is offered as an alternative, but a fix is still proposed. The migration down is only to be checked, with no test of it. Tests are gathered into one step and are not written failing first for each task.

Every task names exact files and starts with a failing test, giving the run command and the expected failure. The migration task includes a test that checks the up and down text. The cleanup conflict gets options a, b and c with a request for the user's answer, but the plan recommends (a) and Task 4 already assumes it, so it does not fully avoid choosing. The tracker and remote claims are backed by command output.

Open question 3 names syncPayments and markPaid as writers of paid_at and plans for them. Task 1 has a down section and a test that asserts the down drops archived_at. Cleanup is raised as a question, but Task 3 already builds option (a), so the attempt chose. Extra findings: the scheduling question and the size-based PR split.

It names sync-payments and markPaid overwriting paid_at and asks the user. The cleanup conflict is left pending ('apply once confirmed') with only a recommendation. It flags sync-payments rewriting paid_at, and the cleanup fix is pending sign-off. The migration round-trip test is conditional on a driver being available ('otherwise verify manually'). On cleanup it says 'This plan assumes that reading' and builds the guard, so it chose instead of leaving the decision to the user. Extra finding: scheduler.

The plan exists only in the reply, with no file written. It flags sync-payments as an edge case for the user. On cleanup it says 'I'll go with A unless you say otherwise', which is a default choice. The plan file passes plan-check and a reviewer pass. Task 1 writes characterization tests for today's overdue behaviour before any source change. The fetch stub is pinned so it never reaches the network. A sent-record (dueSoonSentOn) is planned explicitly in Task 3. The UTC reading is raised as a question. However, no prefactor task adds the seams: the clock (`now`) arrives in the same task as the due-soon feature, and the mailer is never a code seam because tests monkeypatch globalThis.fetch instead.

Task 1 is a pure prefactor that injects `now` and `send` and adds overdue tests before the due-soon feature task. The in-memory sent marker is planned and also flagged as an assumption to confirm. Every test passes a stub `send`, so none sends real email. The UTC reading is flagged rather than imposed. Weakness: the Task 1 overdue test uses the new interface, so it fails first instead of pinning today's behaviour unchanged.

The design puts the now/send seam first. The steps write tests first, including overdue, then the refactor, then the due-soon branch. The sent flag is planned, with retry if a send fails. A fake send means no test reaches real email. The UTC choice is a question to the user. The plan is thin: it is not split into tasks with verify commands, and its step-1 tests depend on an interface that does not exist yet, so the ordering is loose.

There is no prefactor task: one step reworks the whole function, and tests come after the code change, so overdue behaviour is never pinned before the change. The sent marker is planned and fetch is stubbed to throw. However, the plan adds requirements the spec does not state: per-invoice catch, log and continue, plus res.ok checks routed through the overdue path. Both change today's overdue behaviour, against AC 4.

Step 1 is a seam prefactor (now, send), followed by the dedupe marker, fake-send tests and open questions on timezone and persistence. The overdue characterization test runs only after the refactor, so it does not pin today's behaviour before the change. The plan is given only in the reply and no plan file is written.

Task 1 is a prefactor and comes before any feature work. It adds an injectable `now` and pulls a `sendReminder` helper out of the loop. The mail seam is weaker than true injection, because tests still mock the global `fetch`. Task 1 also pins today's overdue behaviour with tests before anything changes (AC 4). The AC 3 sent-record is planned explicitly as a WeakSet, and its process-lifetime limit is raised as an open question. Every test mocks `fetch`, including the failing first run, so no test sends real email. Small invention: the retry-on-failed-send test and the Review Focus behaviour go beyond what the spec states. Remote and config claims are backed by command output.

Step 1 is a refactor that injects `now` and `send` before the due-soon step. The `dueSoonSentAt` sent-record is planned, and its persistence is raised as a question. Tests use a fake `send`, so no real email goes out. However, all tests come after both code changes, so overdue behaviour is never pinned before the change (AC 4 missed). It adds behaviour the spec does not state: a retry on non-2xx (`res.ok`) responses, and dedupe on any later day. The plan has no test-first task structure.

Step 1 is a refactor that adds the `{ send, now }` seam before the feature. The `dueSoonSentAt` record is planned, and the restart risk is noted. Tests use a fake `send`. Tests only come in step 4, after the change, so there is no overdue characterization first. It invents 'log the error and continue with other invoices', which changes current behaviour. It also invents the retry behaviour and a template-check release step.

Tests come first, including overdue unchanged. Then the clock and mailer refactor comes before the due-soon logic. The `dueSoonSentOn` marker is planned, and the persistence and restart risk is raised. Tests use a fake `send`, though tests written before the seam exists could reach the real `fetch` if run before step 2. It invents retry-on-`res.ok` and suggests a new `clearInvoices` production export. The steps are thin, with no exact assertions or failure expectations.

Task 1 injects `now` and `send` and pins the overdue test first. Task 2 adds due-soon, and the `dueSoonSentOn` record is planned with its in-memory limit noted. But Task 1 Step 2 expects the failing run to show 'real fetch attempted', so the planned test run would call the real mail endpoint (b4 missed). It invents requirements the spec does not state: invalid-`dueAt` handling with no throw, the retry semantics, and unrequested commit steps.

Step 1 is a no-behaviour-change refactor that adds the injectable { now, send } before the due-soon branch. The dueSoonSentAt sent-record is planned and its in-memory limit is flagged. Tests use a fake send and a fetch guard that throws. The time-zone and template questions are raised rather than assumed. Misses AC4 ordering: the overdue test is written only after the change. Extra points raised: time zone, overdue repeats, template existence.

The seam is in the design, but the steps do it in one edit together with the feature, so there is no prefactor task. The sent-record is planned and the in-memory assumption is listed. Fake send keeps tests off real email. No test pins overdue behaviour before the edit. It claims that Node runs each test file in its own process, and no command shows that.

Task 1 pins today's overdue behaviour behind a fetch stub before any change, which satisfies AC4 well. The sent-record is planned and persistence is an open question. The fetch stub was checked on the real Node version, and the reviewer's findings were fixed. There is no clock or mailer seam in the code before the feature: now is added inside the feature task and the mailer stays as global fetch.

The injectable clock and mailer are folded into the same step as the due-soon branch, so there is no separate prefactor. The sent-record is planned. Fake send and a fetch guard keep tests off real email. Tests come after the change, so overdue behaviour is not pinned first. It claims without a command that node --test isolates files in separate processes.

It is a single task with no prefactor, and the seam is written together with the feature. The failing tests, including the overdue one, come before the implementation, and the sent-record is planned. But Step 3 runs the tests before the seam exists and expects the real fetch to be called, so a test would send real email. It also invents a requirement that an invalid dueAt must not throw.
